strengths: Well-motivated hypothesis about LLM suggestibility with clear empirical validation in preliminary study (Figure 3)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, FActScore), models, and settings (short/long-form, gray/black-box)
Consistent and substantial calibration improvements (0.099 ECE on TriviaQA, 0.092 on SimpleQA, 0.072-0.074 correlation on FActScore)
Identifies and quantifies underexplored confidence saturation problem with novel Δε metric
Thorough ablations demonstrating necessity of components (Table 5: NLI is crucial; Figure 4: scaling SC alone insufficient)
Practical applicability in zero-resource settings with both gray-box and black-box variants
Robustness across model architectures and confidence formats (Appendix D.1)
weaknesses: Theoretical model makes strong unvalidated assumptions (β(c) approximately equal for logically-related claims; no empirical verification of Eq. 1 assumptions)
Distractor generation lacks principled design: K=5 chosen without ablation; beam search may not generate representative alternatives; black-box prompting not analyzed
Method combines three components (normalization, NLI, self-consistency) with limited analysis of interactions; 50-50 SC/NVC weighting appears arbitrary without ablation
Dependence on external NLI model introduces failure point; limited sensitivity analysis to NLI quality or choice of model
Computational cost not discussed (10 forward passes); comparison claiming 'DINCO at 10 calls beats SC at 100' somewhat misleading as different budgets
Missing ablations on key hyperparameters: number of distractors K, beam search size, sensitivity to mutual exclusivity assumption
Inconsistency between problem and solution: paper shows β(C)>1 indicates miscalibration but doesn't validate that normalization recovers true probabilities
Limited failure case analysis; black-box performance on SimpleQA shows notable drops (0.605 vs 0.786 AUC) not deeply discussed
FActScore correlation improvements moderate (0.518-0.724 range); practical significance unclear
No evaluation on downstream tasks to validate claim that desaturation produces 'more usable' confidence estimates

strengths: Clear identification and empirical validation of suggestibility problem; preliminary study (Fig. 3) shows higher total confidence on incorrect answers
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, FActScore), models (open/closed-source), metrics (ECE, Brier, AUC), and settings (gray-box/black-box)
Consistent calibration improvements with better saturation properties; DINCO achieves Δ₀ of 0.998 vs. 0.670 for vanilla VC
Practical applicability and thorough experimental documentation with detailed prompts, significance testing, ablations, and analysis
Strong quantitative results on short-form QA with ECE improvements of ~0.09-0.10 over best baselines and good transfer to long-form generation
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: multi-candidate normalization (Tian et al. 2023, Kadavath et al. 2022) and NLI weighting are known techniques; distinction from related work via independent vs. joint prompting is primarily an implementation detail

Weak theoretical foundation: assumes uniform β(c) across claims and probabilistic coherence without validation; causality of suggestibility is inferred from correlation with correctness; lacks sensitivity analysis for key assumptions

Method complexity understated: requires NLI model (making it non-zero-resource; Table 5 shows ECE drops 0.358→0.171 without it), beam search, SC sampling, and careful prompting; black-box version significantly underperforms (ECE 0.161 vs. 0.089 with logit access)

Experimental concerns: small datasets (1000 samples per short-form task; 183 for long-form); LLM-as-judge evaluation introduces bias; missing direct comparison with Chhikara (2025) which appears conceptually similar; statistical margins sometimes marginal
Incomplete analysis: no failure case studies or case-level analysis; missing ablations on number of distractors, SC samples, and alternative normalizations; NLI error propagation not explored
Long-form results weaker in absolute terms (ECE 0.076 remains substantial); limited to biography generation; generalization to other long-form tasks unclear
Inference cost not transparently analyzed: method requires ~10 calls per example; wall-clock time and API costs not discussed despite claims of efficiency over 100-sample SC

Causal mechanism insufficiently established: uses correctness as proxy for epistemic certainty (acknowledged as imperfect); does not explain why independent prompting with NLI downweighting should substantially outperform joint prompting

strengths: Clear problem identification with well-validated empirical motivation: saturation and overconfidence in verbalized confidence with demonstrated correlation to suggestibility (Figure 3)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple datasets (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, FActScore), models (open/closed-source, varied scales), metrics (ECE/BS/AUC), and rigorous statistical testing with high human agreement (96-99%)
Strong and consistent empirical results: ECE improvements of 0.099 (TriviaQA), 0.092 (SimpleQA), and 0.055 (FActScore) across diverse model architectures

Thorough analysis and ablations: saturation quantification (Table 4), scaling analysis showing SC-100 cannot match DINCO-10 (Figure 4), NLI ablation (Table 5), and robustness to different confidence formats
Practical applicability: zero-resource setting, handles both gray-box and black-box scenarios, seamlessly extends from short-form to long-form tasks
Well-motivated integration of complementary coherence dimensions (generation and validation) with clear theoretical framing through generator-validator disagreement
Strong reproducibility: detailed prompts, full experimental details, promised code release, and high LLM-as-judge agreement with human evaluation
weaknesses: Theoretical assumptions require stronger justification: assumption that bias β(C) is uniform across mutually exclusive alternatives (Eq. 1) is strong and may not hold with heterogeneous uncertainty; multiplicative bias model lacks deep theoretical grounding

Method complexity with under-explored design choices: 50-50 equal weighting of f^SC and f^NVC appears arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; max(1, β(C)) safeguard potentially masks issues; optimal K=5 distractors not validated
Black-box performance substantially degrades (GPT-4.1 ECE: 0.089 gray-box vs 0.161 black-box), indicating method heavily depends on logit access and limiting generality to API-only models
Distractor quality is critical but under-analyzed: no systematic study of failure modes, sensitivity to low-quality distractor generation, or cumulative errors in long-form per-claim generation
Computational cost not fully addressed: requires ~10+ forward passes per instance; while DINCO-10 beats SC-100, absolute inference cost is substantial with no wall-clock timing analysis
Limited novelty in individual components: normalizing over multiple candidates and self-consistency are existing ideas; primary contribution is combining them, which feels somewhat incremental

Evaluation limitations: ECE with 10 bins is coarse; SimpleQA only 914 examples after exclusions; FActScore only 183 entities; missing temperature scaling baselines; no out-of-distribution or failure case analysis
Assumptions about mutual exclusivity and exhaustiveness may not hold broadly; unclear how DINCO handles overlapping or non-exhaustive alternatives despite NLI-based weighting attempt
Missing practical guidance: no recommended confidence thresholds; long-form correlation improvements (0.072-0.074) are modest with unclear practical significance

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing two underexplored issues in verbalized confidence: overconfidence and saturation, with empirical support for the suggestibility hypothesis
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Qwen, Llama, Gemma, GPT-4.1, Gemini), datasets (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, FactScore), and settings (gray-box, black-box)
Consistent improvements across all major experiments with proper statistical significance testing, demonstrating generalizability of the approach
Thorough analysis and ablations including saturation quantification, scaling studies, NLI ablation, and robustness to hyperparameters and model choices
Practical considerations addressed including black-box settings, efficiency variants, and potential for smaller model distractor generation
Clear presentation with effective figures (particularly Figures 1-2) and well-organized narrative with informative appendices
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core idea of normalizing confidence over multiple answers builds directly on existing work (Tian et al. 2023, Kadavath et al. 2022); claimed distinction between independent vs. joint prompting lacks direct experimental comparison

Weak theoretical foundation: assumptions in Eq. 1-2 (coherent latent confidence, uniform bias across related claims) are plausible but unvalidated; max(1, β(C)) adjustment appears ad-hoc; 50-50 weighting of SC and NVC lacks principled justification

Suggestibility hypothesis relies on correctness as noisy proxy for epistemic certainty; causal relationship between suggestibility and overconfidence not rigorously established; alternative explanations (e.g., instruction-tuning artifacts) not thoroughly ruled out

Methodological dependencies: NLI model requirement contradicts zero-resource claims despite Appendix D.3 robustness testing; quality and diversity of self-generated distractors rely on beam search heuristics without coverage guarantees

Mixed results in some settings: SimpleQA (GPT-4.1) shows DINCO AUC=0.786 vs MSP=0.800; FactScore improvements modest (avg 0.055); computational overhead of 10-32% may be prohibitive for some applications

Limited failure analysis: no discussion of failure modes, worst-case scenarios, or question types with minimal improvement; evaluation concerns include 86 excluded SimpleQA refusals and only 1000 samples per dataset

strengths: Clear problem identification: Identifies and empirically validates the suggestibility phenomenon (higher confidence on incorrect questions) as a source of miscalibration in verbalized confidence
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, FactScore, BioASQ), models, and metrics with proper statistical significance testing
Consistent practical improvements: ECE reductions of 0.077-0.092 across tasks; works in both gray-box and black-box settings
Thoughtful engineering: Addresses practical challenges (claim redundancy via weighted measures, multiple distractor strategies, one-step efficiency variant)
Thorough reproducibility: Detailed prompts, evaluation procedures, extensive ablations, and supplementary analyses
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core contribution (normalizing VC by sum of confidences on distractors) is straightforward; applies known phenomena (suggestibility) directly without deep insight

Weak theoretical foundation: Strong assumptions in Eq. 2 (equal β across related claims, probabilistic coherence of f^lat) lack rigorous justification; no analysis of when/why these hold; causality between suggestibility and proposed solution unclear

Critical NLI dependency undermined: While claimed as 'minimal departure from zero-resource,' NLI errors propagate substantially (Table 5: -0.228 ECE without NLI); limited analysis of robustness to contradiction detection failures

No failure case analysis: Lacks systematic identification of when method breaks down, worst-case scenarios, result variance analysis, or performance on non-factual tasks (reasoning, code, creative writing)
Modest improvements: ECE reductions of 0.08-0.09 are incremental; DINCO costs 32% more FLOPs than SC; improvements are consistent but not transformative for a top-tier venue

Narrow evaluation scope: Only factual QA/biography tasks; generalization beyond knowledge-intensive domains unexplored; missing comparisons to training-based calibration and recent uncertainty quantification work

Loose 'suggestibility' framing: Uses correctness as noisy proxy for epistemic certainty (Section 2.2); higher total confidence on incorrect questions could arise from misconceptions or systematic biases, not just suggestibility
Ad-hoc design choices: Why normalize by sum vs. max/mean? Why equal budget split? Sensitivity not explored; max(1, β(C)) modification reverts to vanilla VC when no true claim exists

strengths: Clear problem motivation with empirically-validated hypothesis about LLM suggestibility on unfamiliar topics
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, FactScore), models (Qwen, Llama, Gemma, GPT-4.1, Gemini), and metrics (ECE, Brier Score, AUC, Pearson/Spearman correlation)
Consistent and substantial calibration improvements (0.055-0.092 ECE reduction) across all evaluated settings
Rigorous ablation studies demonstrating importance of each component (NLI weighting reduces ECE 0.171→0.358, saturation analysis quantifies improvement)
Scaling analysis showing SC cannot match DINCO even at 100 samples despite 7.6× higher computational cost
Practical applicability with no training required, works in both gray-box and black-box settings, uses lightweight off-the-shelf NLI model
Excellent reproducibility with detailed prompts, hyperparameters, extensive distractor examples, and analysis of generation methods
Clean mathematical formulation of suggestibility bias as multiplicative factor and coherent integration of generation/validation signals
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core normalization idea (Eq. 2) is straightforward application of probabilistic coherence, NLI-based weighting is standard, and self-consistency is from prior work; main contribution is the empirical validation of their combination

Substantial black-box performance gap: DINCOblack-box achieves ECE 0.161 vs DINCO 0.089 on GPT-4.1 (Table 2), ~1.8× worse calibration, significantly limiting real-world applicability for API-only models

Distractor quality dependency incompletely addressed: mutual exclusivity not guaranteed by design, quality depends on model's uncertain epistemic state, and no empirical analysis of correlation between distractor quality metrics and final calibration performance

Limited evaluation scope: tested only on factual correctness tasks (QA, biography generation); generalization to other domains (summarization, translation) or tasks with multiple equally-valid answers unclear

Strong assumptions in mathematical framework not fully justified: assumes β(c) roughly equal for logically related claims (Eq. 1); max(1, β(C)) defaulting in Eq. 4 is somewhat ad-hoc; 50-50 SC/NVC weighting appears arbitrary
Saturation addressed as symptom rather than root cause: paper doesn't explain fundamental source of saturation in instruction-tuned models or propose architectural fixes
No failure case analysis or error analysis: when would DINCO perform poorly? When distractor quality is low? How sensitive is method to distractor generation quality?
NLI model dependency conflicts with 'zero-resource' claims: despite being off-the-shelf, introduces external dependency; weights w_unique and w_contra lack clear justification
